description: Performance and resource metrics for kube-shard components: secondary API server (KAS), Kine storage layer, and PostgreSQL database.

panels.description:
Total SQL operations per second across all Kine query types, stacked by operation name.

**Key operations:**
- **GetSingleVal**: Point reads — the hottest path (watch + get)
- **AfterAllOldVal**: Watch polling (list changes after a revision)
- **CompactRev**: Revision compaction lookups
- **Insert**: Writes (create/update/delete resources)
- **ListCurrentVal**: List operations (informer initial list)
- **GetRevisionAfterVal**: Watch continuation queries
- **CountCurrent**: Count queries
- **GetSize**: Database size checks
- **Compact**: Actual compaction deletes
panels.title: SQL Operations Rate (by type)

panels.description: p50, p95, and p99 SQL query latencies across all operations. High latencies indicate PostgreSQL performance issues or connection pool saturation.
panels.title: SQL Latency Percentiles (All Operations)

panels.description: Current total of successful compaction cycles. Compaction removes old revisions from the database to prevent unbounded growth.
panels.title: Total Compactions

panels.description: Rate of SQL errors. Error code 23505 is a PostgreSQL unique constraint violation (optimistic concurrency conflict) — these are expected and retried. Other errors may indicate database issues.
panels.title: SQL Error Rate

panels.description: Insert errors not retried internally by Kine's serial-ID conflict loop. These are typically legitimate unique constraint violations (e.g., optimistic concurrency conflicts) that surface as HTTP 409 to the API server and are retried at a higher level. Non-zero values are normal under concurrent writes.
panels.title: Non-Retriable Insert Errors
Read Path — Watches & Gets power the Kubernetes informer cache. High latency here directly impacts controller responsiveness.

panels.description: Watch polling latency (AfterAllOldVal). This is the core watch loop query — Kine polls PostgreSQL for rows inserted after a given revision. p99 above 10ms under load warrants investigation.
panels.title: Watch Poll Latency (AfterAllOldVal)

panels.description: Point-read latency (GetSingleVal). Used for individual resource GETs. This is the highest-volume operation — even small regressions multiply quickly.
panels.title: Get Latency (GetSingleVal)

panels.description: List operation latency (ListCurrentVal). Used by informer initial list and re-list after watch failures. High latency causes slow controller startup.
panels.title: List Latency (ListCurrentVal)

panels.description: Read operation rates broken down by type. Helps identify which read path is under pressure.
panels.title: Read Operations Rate (by type)
Write Path — Inserts create new revisions for resource creates/updates/deletes. Write latency directly impacts kubectl apply and controller reconciliation speed.

panels.description: Insert latency percentiles. Each Kubernetes write (create, update, delete) becomes one or more Insert operations. p99 above 50ms under load may indicate PostgreSQL write contention.
panels.title: Insert Latency

panels.description: Insert rate vs conflict rate. Conflicts (error 23505) are expected under concurrent writes — Kine uses optimistic locking. A high conflict ratio (>10%) means heavy write contention on the same keys.
panels.title: Insert Rate vs Conflicts
Compaction — Removes old revisions to prevent database bloat. If compaction falls behind, the kine table grows unbounded, degrading query performance.

panels.description: Compaction rate — how often compaction cycles run. Should be steady. Drops indicate compaction is stalled or the process is unhealthy.
panels.title: Compaction Rate

panels.description: Compaction SQL latency. The Compact operation deletes old rows, CompactRev looks up which revisions to compact. Rising latency means the table is growing or indexes need maintenance.
panels.title: Compaction Latency (p99)

panels.description: Ratio of insert rate to compaction rate. If this ratio grows over time, compaction is not keeping up with writes and the database will bloat.
panels.title: Insert to Compact Ratio
Resources — Container-level resource usage for Kine pods

panels.description: Goroutine count over time. A steady upward trend indicates a goroutine leak.
panels.title: Goroutines (over time)

panels.description: Container memory working set per Kine pod. Compare with resource limits to assess headroom.
panels.title: Kine Memory (Working Set)

panels.description: Container CPU usage per Kine pod in cores.
panels.title: Kine CPU Usage
Secondary API Server (KAS) — The aggregated kube-apiserver serving sharded API groups. Resource pressure here affects all API requests for sharded resources.

panels.description: Number of objects stored per resource type. Shows the top 10 by count. Large resource counts (e.g., TaskRuns) drive memory usage in both KAS watch caches and Kine.
panels.title: Top Resources by Object Count

panels.description: Object count over time for the top stored resources. Lines that grow without plateauing indicate garbage collection or cleanup is not working — resources are accumulating unbounded. Healthy behavior: lines plateau or oscillate as creates are balanced by deletes.
panels.title: Resource Object Count Over Time

panels.description: Incoming API request rate broken down by verb. GET dominates (informer-driven). High APPLY/PUT indicates active reconciliation. WATCH connections are long-lived, so the rate appears low even with many active watches.
panels.title: API Request Rate by Verb

panels.description: Number of active long-running requests (primarily watches). Each watch holds a goroutine and memory in the KAS watch cache. Growth correlates with controllers connecting to the secondary. A sudden drop may indicate a network partition or KAS restart.
panels.title: Active Watches by Resource

panels.description: API request latency at p99 for each verb (WATCH excluded). LIST latency depends on the number of objects returned; GET should stay sub-100ms. Rising latency indicates Kine backend pressure or resource exhaustion.
panels.title: API Request Latency (p99 by Verb)

panels.description: Rate of 4xx/5xx responses from the secondary KAS. 409 (Conflict) is normal under concurrent updates. 429 means flow control throttling. 500+ indicates server-side errors worth investigating.
panels.title: API Error Rate by Status Code

panels.description: SubjectAccessReview webhook latency (p99). The secondary KAS delegates authorization to the primary cluster via webhook. This latency is added to every API request. High values (>100ms) indicate primary KAS pressure or network issues.
panels.title: Authorization Webhook Latency

panels.description: Container memory working set per KAS pod. Compare with resource limits to assess OOM risk. The secondary KAS caches informer data and holds open watch connections.
panels.title: KAS Memory (Working Set)

panels.description: Container CPU usage per KAS pod in cores. High CPU may indicate excessive request volume or expensive list operations.
panels.title: KAS CPU Usage

panels.description: Container restarts for KAS pods. Restarts may indicate OOMKills, liveness probe failures, or crash loops.
panels.title: KAS Container Restarts
PostgreSQL Resources — Container-level CPU, memory, disk, and restarts. Pressure here cascades into higher SQL latencies for both reads and writes.

panels.description: Container memory working set per PostgreSQL pod. PostgreSQL uses shared_buffers and OS page cache heavily — sustained growth may indicate bloated tables or missing vacuums.
panels.title: PostgreSQL Memory (Working Set)

panels.description: Container CPU usage per PostgreSQL pod in cores. High CPU typically correlates with increased SQL query volume or expensive compaction deletes.
panels.title: PostgreSQL CPU Usage

panels.description: PostgreSQL PVC disk usage vs capacity. Sustained growth towards capacity means compaction is not keeping up or the PVC needs to be expanded.
panels.title: PostgreSQL PVC Usage

panels.description: Container restarts for PostgreSQL pods. Restarts cause temporary Kine connection failures and watch disruptions.
panels.title: PostgreSQL Container Restarts
PostgreSQL Storage — Live vs reclaimable space (includes TOAST, where Kine stores resource bodies). High reclaimable bytes mean compaction/VACUUM is not returning disk to the OS.

panels.description:
Database size vs table composition from pgstattuple_approx (regular + TOAST tables).

- **db_size**: pg_database_size — whole database including indexes, FSM, and WAL leftovers
- **tables_size**: on-disk size of user tables (live + dead + free)
- **live**: approximate bytes in live tuples (current Kine data)
- **reclaimable**: dead tuples + free space (returned only by VACUUM FULL / CLUSTER, not regular VACUUM)

If reclaimable grows while live is flat, Kine compaction is deleting rows but PostgreSQL has not yet compacted the heap/TOAST files.
panels.title: Database Size (Live vs Reclaimable)

panels.description: Fraction of table bytes that are dead tuples or free space (reclaimable / tables_size). Above ~50% means most of the on-disk kine/TOAST data is wasted; consider more aggressive Kine compaction or a one-shot VACUUM FULL during a maintenance window. This is an approximate gauge updated every bloatInterval (default 5m).
panels.title: Table Bloat Ratio

panels.description: Estimated live vs dead heap tuples from pg_stat_user_tables (not TOAST). Dead heap tuples are what regular VACUUM can mark reusable. If dead rows climb, autovacuum is falling behind Kine's insert/delete rate — tune autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor / autovacuum_vacuum_threshold on the kine table. TOAST bloat will not show up here; use the size/bloat panels for that.
panels.title: Heap Tuples (Live vs Dead)
PostgreSQL Buffer Cache — Hit ratio by page type. Kine resource bodies live in TOAST; a low TOAST hit ratio means shared_buffers is too small for the working set and queries wait on disk.

panels.description: Heap buffer cache hit ratio: heap_hit / (heap_hit + heap_read). Target ≥99% for OLTP. Lower values mean table pages are not staying in shared_buffers.
panels.title: Heap Cache Hit

panels.description: Index buffer cache hit ratio: idx_hit / (idx_hit + idx_read). Kine's GetSingleVal / AfterAllOldVal paths are index-heavy. Target ≥99%.
panels.title: Index Cache Hit

panels.description: TOAST buffer cache hit ratio: toast_hit / (toast_hit + toast_read). This is the most important cache metric for kube-shard — Kine stores resource YAML in a TOAST column. A low ratio (this cluster was ~76%) means PipelineRun bodies are read from disk; raise shared_buffers or reduce live data.
panels.title: TOAST Cache Hit

panels.description: TOAST index cache hit ratio: tidx_hit / (tidx_hit + tidx_read). The TOAST index maps chunk_id to TOAST pages. Should stay high even when TOAST heap pages miss.
panels.title: TOAST Index Cache Hit

panels.description: Buffer cache hit ratio over time for heap, indexes, TOAST, and TOAST indexes. Use this to size shared_buffers: if TOAST stays below ~95% while indexes are fine, the working set of resource bodies does not fit in cache. Correlate drops with SQL p99 and PostgreSQL CPU.
panels.title: Cache Hit Ratio by Page Type

panels.description: Disk block reads (cache misses) per second by page type. toast_read is the signal that Kine is fetching resource bodies from disk. Rising heap_read/idx_read with flat QPS means the cache is being evicted (shared_buffers too small, or checkpoints flushing too hard).
panels.title: Disk Block Reads (Cache Misses)
PostgreSQL Activity — Connections, transactions, row ops, and checkpoints. Use these to size max_connections / Kine pool and to catch checkpoint storms that spike CPU and kill cache hit ratio.

panels.description: Backends vs max_connections. Kine opens a pool of SQL connections; each Kine replica adds more. If backends approach max, new Kine queries block on connection acquisition — raise max_connections (and memory) or lower Kine pool size. Includes autovacuum workers.
panels.title: Connections vs Max

panels.description: Commit vs rollback rate. Rollbacks are expected from Kine optimistic-concurrency conflicts (SQLSTATE 23505) that abort the transaction. A rollback ratio that tracks the Insert conflict panel is healthy; a spike without matching 23505 errors may indicate statement timeouts (e.g. the bloat query) or deadlocks.
panels.title: Commits vs Rollbacks

panels.description: Heap row operations. Kine is append-mostly: Insert creates a new revision, Compact deletes old ones. hot_upd should stay near 0 (Kine does not HOT-update the value column). If ins >> del over a long window, compaction is behind and live+dead rows will grow. Correlate with Kine insert/compact ratio.
panels.title: Row Operations (ins/upd/del)

panels.description: Checkpoint rate by type. scheduled = checkpoint_timeout. requested = max_wal_size hit or CREATE INDEX / explicit checkpoint. If requested approaches or exceeds scheduled, WAL is filling too fast — raise max_wal_size or checkpoint_timeout. Requested storms flush shared_buffers, which tanks the TOAST cache hit ratio and spikes CPU.
panels.title: Checkpoints (Scheduled vs Requested)

panels.description: Time spent in checkpoint write vs fsync, as a rate of milliseconds per second (1000 = checkpoints are busy the whole interval). High write time = dirtying too many buffers between checkpoints (raise checkpoint_timeout / max_wal_size, or more bgwriter). High sync time = slow disk or too much to flush at once (checkpoint_completion_target).
panels.title: Checkpoint Duration (write vs sync)

panels.description: Buffers written by source. checkpoints = checkpoint flushes (expected). bgwriter = background writer keeping pace between checkpoints. backend = backends had to write their own dirty pages (bad — cache eviction under query load). If backend writes rise, increase bgwriter_lru_maxpages / lower bgwriter_delay, or raise shared_buffers so less churn.
panels.title: Buffers Written by Source
